method: The driver (elevated) created the test sublayer S2 and its provider with no filter, a Users-readable folder holding the probe and its arming proof (bound to the exe's own hash, 24 h), and a drop folder the account and the operator could write. The Lead Architect then launched the probe himself: condition F three-plus times as the account through Windows' secondary logon (a filtered token), condition E through an elevation request made from inside the account's own console, condition S from his own non-elevated console, condition A from his elevated console. Each run read its own token (user SID, every group with attributes, integrity, elevation type, linked token), checked the stale SID resolves to no account, then made ONE FwpmFilterAdd0 (persistent block in S2 keyed to the stale SID, fixed key), a read-back, ONE FwpmFilterDeleteByKey0, a read-back, and wrote a record. -Collect validated every record (schema, hashes, condition, account, token state per condition, clock window) and -Finish removed everything by key and verified by direct reads and a netsh export. The account was created, enabled, removed from the group, deleted and its profile deleted by the Lead Architect in Windows' own tools; no script touched any account.

results.engine_access_list: read by netsh wfp show security type=engine at -Prepare and -Finish, identical; the group's ACE (A;;0x307ff;;;NO) present as on 2026-10-13
results.reading: On this build, membership of Network Configuration Operators does not change what a normally launched process can do to the engine: its token carries the group marked deny-only, exactly like a filtered administrator token, and the engine refuses the add. The account's full token, the only one in which the group's ACE would apply, is not reachable through the over-the-shoulder elevation prompt. This is the behaviour Microsoft documents for the four split-token groups; it is not a finding.
